<h1>Research</h1>

<p class="lede">Many questions in statistics and machine learning come down to drawing random samples from a complicated probability distribution. I study Langevin algorithms, which are Markov chain Monte Carlo methods that do this by simulating a random walk guided by the shape of the distribution. My work proves how quickly these samplers converge and designs versions that scale to networks of computers, respect constraints, and use higher-order dynamics to move faster.</p>

<ul class="r-areas">
<li><span class="n">I</span><div><b>Decentralized sampling.</b> <span class="d">Agents on a network learn a shared posterior without pooling their data.</span></div></li>
<li><span class="n">II</span><div><b>Constrained and singular dynamics.</b> <span class="d">Samplers that stay inside a domain and avoid collisions.</span></div></li>
<li><span class="n">III</span><div><b>High-order Langevin Monte Carlo.</b> <span class="d">Faster mixing from higher-order dynamics, with Wasserstein guarantees.</span></div></li>
<li><span class="n">IV</span><div><b>Financial engineering.</b> <span class="d">Time-series prediction, derivative pricing, and risk.</span></div></li>
</ul>  

:::

<div><h2 id="how-it-works">How a Langevin sampler works</h2>
<p>A short, hands-on introduction for anyone new to the topic.</p></div>
:::

Suppose we want random numbers whose histogram follows a given curve. In this example the target is a mixture of two familiar bell curves (normal distributions), one centred at $-1$ that holds 60% of the probability and one centred at $1.2$ that holds the other 40%:

$$\pi(x) \;=\; 0.6\cdot\frac{1}{0.7\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x+1)^2}{2(0.7)^2}} \;+\; 0.4\cdot\frac{1}{0.6\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-1.2)^2}{2(0.6)^2}} .$$

We can write this formula down and evaluate it at any point, but there is no direct way to draw random numbers from it. A Langevin sampler gets around this with walkers that take small random steps guided by the shape of $\pi$.

::: {.steps3}
::: {.step3}
<span class="k">1</span>
<h3>Turn probability into a landscape</h3>
<p>Define the height $U(x) = -\log \pi(x)$. Where $\pi$ is large, $U$ is low, so likely values become valleys and unlikely values become hills.</p>
:::
::: {.step3}
<span class="k">2</span>
<h3>Roll downhill, with random kicks</h3>
<p>At every step each walker takes a small step downhill and then gets a random push. The pull keeps it near likely values, and the kicks keep it from settling in one place.</p>
:::
::: {.step3}
<span class="k">3</span>
<h3>Record where it has been</h3>
<p>Every position a walker visits is one sample. With the right balance of pull and kicks, the histogram of all the samples settles onto $\pi(x)$.</p>
:::
:::

<div class="demo">
<canvas id="langevin-demo" aria-label="Interactive demonstration: on the left, walkers move on the landscape U(x); on the right, a histogram of their positions builds up and approaches the target curve"></canvas>
<div class="demo-bar"><span class="stat"><span data-demo-step>step 0</span> · <span data-demo-count>0 samples</span></span><div class="ctl"><button type="button" data-demo-toggle aria-pressed="true">Pause</button><button type="button" class="kick" data-demo-kick aria-pressed="true">Random kicks: on</button><button type="button" data-demo-reset>Restart</button></div></div>
</div>
<p class="demo-msg" data-demo-msg>Thirty walkers start high on the right-hand slope. Watch them roll into the valleys while the histogram fills in.</p>

::: {.demo-foot}
::: {.math-card}
<p><b>The update rule.</b> With step size $h = 0.03$ and a fresh standard normal draw $\xi_k$ for each walker,</p>
$$x_{k+1} = x_k \;\underbrace{-\,h\,U'(x_k)}_{\text{downhill pull}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k}_{\text{random kick}} .$$
<p><b>How many samples?</b> The demo runs 30 walkers side by side. Each step moves every walker once and records its new position, so each step adds <b>30 samples</b>, and after $k$ steps the histogram holds $30k$.</p>
:::

::: {}
<p>Turn the kicks off and every walker stops at the bottom of its nearest valley. That is gradient descent: it finds a single best point but loses the spread of the distribution. With the kicks on, the walkers keep exploring and occasionally cross the hill between the valleys, so each valley ends up with its correct share: about 60% on the left and 40% on the right.</p>
<p>My research asks how quickly this happens, and how to keep it fast and accurate in high dimensions, across networks of computers, and inside constrained regions.</p>
:::
:::
:::

<div><h2>Current project</h2></div>
:::

<article class="project">
<a class="pmedia" href="research/singular-langevin/"><img class="th-light" src="research/singular-langevin/singular-langevin.png" alt="Simulation: particles following Langevin dynamics inside an elliptical constraint set while repelling one another"><img class="th-dark" src="research/singular-langevin/singular-langevin-dark.png" alt="" aria-hidden="true"></a>
<div class="pbody">
<span class="status-pill">In progress · 2026</span>
<h3><a href="research/singular-langevin/">Constrained Langevin Dynamics with Singular Repulsion</a></h3>
<div class="with">With David P. Herzog, Iowa State University</div>
<p>Particles diffuse inside a bounded region while strongly repelling one another at short range. Standard numerical steps can push them toward collisions, and projecting back can create collisions of its own. We are developing a tamed-proximal Langevin scheme that handles the singular repulsion directly while respecting the boundary, with guarantees on stability, collision avoidance, and convergence.</p>
<div class="foot"><ul class="chips"><li>Well-posedness</li><li>Invariant measures</li><li>Stable discretization</li></ul><a class="text-link" href="research/singular-langevin/">Project overview</a></div>
</div>
</article>
:::

<div class="venue">arXiv:2605.00723</div>
<p class="summary">A decentralized sampler for log-concave distributions on convex domains. A shared proximal regularization based on the Moreau–Yosida envelope lets agents respect the constraint without exchanging private data. Non-asymptotic 2-Wasserstein guarantees cover both individual agents and network averages and quantify the bias introduced by the proximal approximation.</p>
